strengths: Clear, intuitive, and principled formulation: Defining Visual Information Gain (VIG) via the reduction in prediction uncertainty (cross-entropy / KL divergence) between multimodal and visually-deprived inputs is well-motivated and mathematically sound.

Dual-level selection mechanism: The framework applies visual selectivity at both the sample and token levels in a unified manner by reusing the sample threshold \(\tau_p\), avoiding unnecessary hyperparameter proliferation while isolating visually grounded tokens.

Strong empirical efficiency and performance: Across LLaVA-1.5 (7B, 13B) and ShareGPT4V (7B), VIG-guided training consistently matches or surpasses full-data training on both perception benchmarks (LLaVA-W, MMVet, MMBench, DocVQA) and hallucination benchmarks (POPE, CHAIR, MMHal) despite backpropagating on up to 79% fewer tokens.

Orthogonality with existing methods: The paper effectively demonstrates that VIG-guided training can be seamlessly combined with existing inference-time debiasing techniques (VCD, PAI, VAR) and architectural modifications (LACING) to provide additive improvements.

In-depth qualitative and mechanistic analyses: The paper provides insightful supporting evaluations, including visual token attention ratios across network depth, robustness against misleading textual corruption ('blind faith in text'), and clear token-level case studies.
weaknesses: Evaluation on relatively older model architectures: The empirical validation is conducted primarily on the LLaVA-1.5 and ShareGPT4V suites (Vicuna backbones with fixed CLIP visual resolution). Validating the approach on more recent and widely-used architectures (such as Qwen2-VL, InternVL-2/2.5, or LLaVA-OneVision) with dynamic resolution would significantly strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Upfront computational overhead for VIG scoring: Computing VIG requires evaluating two forward passes (clean and blurred image) over the entire instruction-tuning corpus using the pre-aligned model. Although forward-only and parallelizable, this upfront inference cost should be discussed more explicitly in comparison to the savings during instruction tuning.

Heuristic nature of visual absence simulation: Simulating the absence of visual input via Gaussian blurring—while following prior literature—remains an empirical heuristic. The manuscript lacks an ablation comparing this to other natural baselines, such as omitting image tokens entirely, using zero/mean embeddings, or using black images.

Sensitivity to aggressive filtering on complex reasoning tasks: As shown in Table E.3, aggressive sample/token filtering (e.g., \(p=30\%\) or \(50\%\)) leads to significant drops on multi-choice reasoning tasks such as MMBench (dropping from ~65.5% down to ~56.5%), suggesting that masking syntactic and structural tokens too aggressively can compromise complex instruction following or reasoning formatting.

strengths: Conceptual clarity and simplicity: The definition of Visual Information Gain (VIG) via cross-entropy / perplexity difference with and without visual conditioning is mathematically intuitive, model-agnostic, and decomposes naturally to token-level loss differences.

Thorough empirical analysis: The paper effectively verifies that VIG identifies visually grounded tokens (colors, actions, attributes) versus syntactic function words, aligns with benchmark visual dependency profiles, and increases attention allocation to visual tokens across layers.

Consistent performance gains with reduced supervision: The proposed VIG-guided selective training at both sample and token levels achieves solid gains across diverse benchmarks (e.g., MMVet, DocVQA, CHAIR, MMHal) while supervising on 34% to 79% fewer tokens compared to standard full-data instruction tuning.

Orthogonality to existing techniques: Table 4 convincingly demonstrates that VIG-based data curation is complementary to inference-time debiasing techniques (VCD, PAI, VAR) and architectural interventions (LACING).
weaknesses: Simulation of visual absence: The paper relies on Gaussian blur to simulate the absence of visual input following Xing et al. [47], but does not provide an ablation or comparison against alternative, standard ways of disabling visual input (e.g., omitting visual tokens entirely, zero/padding visual embeddings, or uniform gray images).

Evaluation limited to older architectures: Experiments are confined to LLaVA-1.5 and ShareGPT4V (Vicuna + CLIP-ViT). Testing whether the same observation holds for modern native multimodal architectures (such as Qwen2-VL or InternVL-2) would significantly strengthen the generality of the findings.

Missing 'Token Selection Only' baseline: Table 5 and Table E.1 compare Random, Sample Selection (SS), and Sample + Token Selection (SS+TS). It is noticeable that SS alone causes a severe drop on MMBench (from 65.46 down to 57.56), which is recovered once TS is added. An ablation exploring Token Selection alone (TS without pruning entire samples) would provide clearer insight into the interaction between sample-level pruning and token masking.

strengths: Sound and well-motivated formulation: Visual Information Gain (VIG) provides an intuitive, theoretically grounded, and decomposable metric based on cross-entropy reduction to quantify visual dependence at both the sample and token levels.

Data-efficient training paradigm: The proposed selective training scheme filters weakly grounded samples and focuses gradient updates exclusively on high-VIG tokens, achieving superior performance on vision understanding and hallucination benchmarks while significantly reducing active training tokens (e.g., up to 79% token reduction in LLaVA-1.5 13B).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across multiple LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V) and benchmark suites (LLaVA-Bench, MMVet, MMBench, DocVQA, POPE, CHAIR, MMHal), demonstrating consistent improvements over vanilla full-data training.

Orthogonality and mechanistic analysis: The method combines additively with both inference-time interventions (VCD, PAI, VAR) and model-level training modifications (LACING). Detailed analyses on visual attention distribution and robustness under textual corruption ('blind faith in text') confirm that VIG training genuinely steers the model toward visual evidence.

Thorough ablations: The ablation studies clearly isolate the distinct contributions of sample-level versus token-level filtering (Table 5 / Table E.1) and systematically explore the impact of the selection threshold ratio p.
weaknesses: Computational overhead of scoring: Computing VIG requires running two forward passes (clean image and blurred image) over the entire instruction-tuning corpus using an aligned model checkpoint prior to instruction tuning. While parallelizable and one-time, this adds non-trivial preprocessing overhead.

Sensitivity to choice of visual absence proxy: The paper relies on a Gaussian-blurred image to simulate the absence of visual information following prior work, but does not investigate how alternative visual-absence representations (e.g., blank images, zeroed visual embeddings, or removing visual tokens entirely) would affect VIG estimation and subsequent training stability.

Heuristic reuse of threshold across sample and token levels: The decision to reuse the sample-level threshold tau_p for token-level selection is designed to avoid hyperparameters, but because sample VIG is an average of token VIGs, the distribution of token scores differs substantially from sample averages. Exploring token-level percentile cutoffs or quantile thresholds would provide better theoretical and empirical justification.

Limited architectural diversity: Experiments are restricted to LLaVA-1.5 and ShareGPT4V (CLIP vision encoders paired with Vicuna). Validating whether VIG generalizes to newer architectures with dynamic visual resolution or native vision-language tokens (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL2) remains unverified.

strengths: Principled and intuitive concept: Formulating Visual Information Gain (VIG) as the difference in token/sample cross-entropy loss between visually conditioned and unconditioned inputs directly addresses the root cause of language shortcut learning in LVLM instruction tuning.

Insightful fine-grained analysis: The decomposition of VIG to the token level and the subsequent POS and qualitative analyses convincingly show that VIG isolates genuinely visual tokens (attributes, colors, spatial relations) from syntactic function words.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: Evaluated across four distinct LVLM configurations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, and Open-Qwen2VL 2B) and numerous benchmarks (LLaVAW, MMVet, MMBench, CV-Bench, DocVQA, POPE, CHAIR, MMHal), VIG-guided training achieves superior accuracy and lower hallucination rates while using 34% to 79% fewer active training tokens.

Orthogonal and complementary: The approach demonstrates clear compatibility and additive gains when combined with popular inference-time debiasing techniques (e.g., VCD, PAI, VAR) as well as architectural modifications (LACING).

Thorough diagnostics: The paper includes meaningful supplementary analyses, verifying increased visual attention allocation in middle layers, heightened resistance to adversarial textual corruption, preservation of pure LLM capabilities on NLP benchmarks, and stable long-tail category retention.
weaknesses: Heuristic threshold sharing between sample and token levels: The decision to reuse the sample-level threshold $\tau_p$ directly for token-level filtering ($VIG_{i,t} \ge \tau_p$) lacks formal justification. Because $VIG_i$ is an average across sequence length $T_i$, the variance and distribution of individual token gains $VIG_{i,t}$ differ substantially from sample-level means. An ablation or sensitivity analysis comparing this shared threshold against token-specific percentile cutoffs is missing.

Sensitivity to visual absence simulation: To compute the unconditioned perplexity, the method applies Gaussian blurring to the image following Xing et al. (2025). The manuscript lacks analysis of how sensitive VIG scores and training outcomes are to the choice of blur parameters versus other visual removal baselines (e.g., mean pixel replacement, complete token dropping, or pure text-only forward passes).

Compute overhead vs. training efficiency trade-off: While the method reduces gradient backpropagation tokens during instruction tuning, calculating VIG requires two forward passes (original and blurred images) across the full multimodal dataset using the aligned model. A more explicit accounting of total GPU hours (scoring overhead + reduced training time vs. standard training time) would clarify the net computational efficiency.

strengths: Clear, intuitive, and theoretically grounded formulation: Visual Information Gain (VIG) directly quantifies the visual contribution at both sample and token levels via cross-entropy / perplexity reduction, offering an interpretable data-centric diagnostic for multimodal learning.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across multiple distinct model families and sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, and Open-Qwen2VL 2B) on eight diverse benchmarks covering both vision understanding and hallucination mitigation.

Strong data efficiency and performance: Training on high-VIG samples and selectively masking non-informative tokens reduces active supervision tokens by up to 79% while matching or outperforming full-data vanilla baselines.

Thorough and insightful analyses: The paper provides extensive diagnostic studies, including token-level POS distributions, attention weight fractions across layers, robustness under adversarial textual corruption ('blind faith in text'), and preservation of pure text-only LLM capabilities.
weaknesses: Threshold sharing heuristic: Directly reusing the sample-level threshold $\tau_p$ for token-level filtering is an ad-hoc heuristic. Since sample-level VIG is an average across sequence length, its distribution differs substantially from individual token loss differences, which typically exhibit much higher variance. The paper would benefit from evaluating alternative token selection schemes (e.g., independent token-level percentiles or per-sample top-k tokens).

Sensitivity to visual absence simulation: VIG computation relies on a Gaussian-blurred image to simulate the absence of visual evidence. The paper lacks ablation or sensitivity analysis regarding alternative visual degradation strategies (e.g., solid gray/black images, Gaussian noise, or completely omitting image tokens from the prompt).

Overall compute trade-off: Although the fine-tuning phase is more token-efficient, computing VIG requires two forward passes (clean and blurred) across the entire multimodal instruction dataset using the aligned model prior to instruction tuning. A more explicit accounting of total end-to-end compute would provide a clearer operational comparison against standard training.

strengths: Principled and intuitive formulation: The paper introduces Visual Information Gain (VIG) as a cross-entropy / perplexity difference between vision-conditioned and visually-ablated states, naturally decomposing into both sample-level and token-level visual grounding metrics.

Strong empirical results and data efficiency: Across four LVLM configurations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, and Open-Qwen2VL 2B), VIG-guided selective training improves vision understanding and significantly lowers hallucination rates while pruning 30% of training samples and up to 34%–79% of active token supervision.

Comprehensive evaluation and diagnostic analysis: The paper includes a wide variety of benchmarks (five visual reasoning, three hallucination, and four text-only benchmarks), along with thorough diagnostic analyses including token POS distribution, cross-layer visual attention allocation, resistance to adversarial text corruption ('blind faith in text'), and long-tail concept retention.

Demonstrated orthogonality: The method operates at the data/supervision level and demonstrates strong compatibility and additive gains when paired with both inference-time debiasing techniques (VCD, PAI, VAR) and architectural training methods (LACING).
weaknesses: Offline computational overhead: Calculating VIG requires two forward passes (clean and blurred images) across the full multimodal instruction dataset using the aligned model prior to instruction tuning, adding non-trivial preprocessing compute.

Heuristic visual absence simulation: Simulating the absence of visual information through Gaussian blur relies on specific filter parameters; comparing against other visual ablation strategies (e.g., pure black/blank image, random noise, or zeroing visual embeddings) would provide a stronger justification.

Coupled sample-and-token threshold heuristic: The decision to apply the sample-level cutoff threshold tau_p directly to token-level filtering avoids extra hyperparameters, but sample averages and per-token loss differences have distinct distribution shapes, making this coupling somewhat arbitrary without deeper theoretical justification.

Static evaluation without curriculum: VIG is calculated statically once using the pretrained alignment checkpoint; the paper does not explore whether visual dependency dynamics shift during instruction tuning or whether iterative/curriculum-based scoring would offer advantages.
